items.name: Champagne
clues: Fizzy, expensive and usually opened when somebody has something to celebrate.
A region in north-eastern France, around the cities of Reims and Épernay.
Only wine from that region, made with a second fermentation inside the bottle, may use the name.
In 2021 Russia passed a law saying only Russian producers could use the Russian word for it. French bottles had to say “sparkling wine” instead.
Its bottles are so thick because the pressure inside is about three times that of a car tyre.
It has the same name as the region. A German version would be called Sekt.

items.name: Parmigiano Reggiano
clues: Hard, salty and crumbly, and usually grated over pasta.
A few provinces of northern Italy, including Parma and Reggio Emilia.
It must be aged for at least twelve months, and each wheel weighs about 40 kilos.
In 2008 the EU’s highest court ruled that its well-known shorter name brings the real thing to mind, so imitations in Europe can’t use it.
An Italian bank accepts the wheels as security for loans and keeps them in its own warehouses while they age.
In English and German it is usually just called Parmesan.

items.name: Feta
clues: White, salty and crumbly. It often sits on top of a salad with olives and tomatoes.
Greece, and only Greece.
It must be made from sheep’s milk, with up to 30 per cent goat’s milk allowed.
Germany and Denmark went to the EU’s highest court to go on using the name. In 2005 they lost.
In 2022 the same court ruled that Denmark had broken EU law by letting its dairies sell their own version outside the EU under that name.
A four-letter cheese. A Greek salad isn’t a Greek salad without it.

items.name: Tequila
clues: Strong, clear or golden, and often drunk in one go with salt and a slice of lime.
Mexico, mostly the state of Jalisco.
It must be made from a single plant, the blue agave.
The fields of spiky blue plants around the town it is named after are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Despite the legend, you won’t find a worm in the bottle. That was a marketing trick for a related drink.
It shares its name with a town near Guadalajara, and with a 1958 hit song in which the band only ever shout this one word.

items.name: Prosecco
clues: Light, fizzy and cheap enough for a Tuesday. The British drink enormous amounts of it.
North-eastern Italy, in the hills between Venice and the Alps.
In 2009, to protect the name, the grape it is made from was officially renamed Glera.
Since 2021 Italy has fought Croatia’s request to protect the name of a sweet Croatian dessert wine that sounds almost the same.
It takes its name from a village above Trieste, near the Slovenian border.
Italy’s best-known sparkling wine, and the fizz in an Aperol Spritz.

items.name: Harris Tweed
clues: Warm, rough and hard-wearing. Your grandfather’s best jacket might be made of it.
The Outer Hebrides, the islands off the north-west coast of Scotland.
By law it must be woven by hand, in the islanders’ own homes, from pure new wool that was dyed and spun on the islands.
It is protected by its own Act of Parliament, passed in 1993.
Its orb logo was first registered in 1909, which makes it the oldest British certification mark.
A woollen cloth named after the island of Harris.
